On 150 generated instances with 50-150 nodes, DG-CGM achieves the optimal cost on 89 of the 91 instances solved to proven optimality by Gurobi, with a geometric mean runtime equal to 5.2% of that for Gurobi and a mean relative cost reduction of 3.4%. On six full-scale scenarios derived from the 2026 INFORMS Railway Applications Section competition data, each with 47,193 nodes, DG-CGM obtains feasible solutions within two hours that serve 95.9%-99.6% of the requested freight volume, providing practical blocking plans for large-scale railway operations. The code, instances, and computational results are publicly available at https://github.com/Zhengzhong-You/IRBP.

items.title: Riemannian Optimization on Unknown Manifolds via Stochastic Proximal Refinement
items.summary: We study Riemannian optimization on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples. The central challenge is to turn feasible samples into optimization steps, i.e., the samples are drawn from the unknown feasible manifold, but do not directly provide the tangent spaces, projections, or retractions required by classic Riemannian methods. Moreover, regions with low objective values may be sparsely represented in the data, so directly sampling from a distribution fitted to these observations can require many draws to find better feasible solutions. We introduce Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds (PRISM), which turns feasible-sample access into an iterative optimization procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. Theoretically, we show that PRISM recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, leading to provable objective descent, feasibility (manifold adherence), and convergence toward first-order stationarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through synthetic experiments illustrating its geometric properties and applications to data-driven building control and diverse real world optimization tasks, highlighting its potential as a general framework for data-driven optimization across scientific and engineering domains.

items.title: Region-Preserving Accelerated Gradient Methods for Geodesically Convex Optimization
items.summary: Accelerated Riemannian optimization methods often require a priori assumptions that their iterates remain in a region where geometric bounds hold. We develop a parameterized inertial dynamical system and an explicit accelerated gradient method for smooth geodesically convex optimization on Riemannian manifolds with locally bounded sectional curvature. Our setting allows both positive and negative curvature without requiring completeness of the ambient manifold. Starting from a curvature-corrected continuous model, we construct the discrete updates by eliminating indefinite cross terms in the Lyapunov energy difference and derive verifiable conditions for a fixed step size. The resulting energy analysis establishes preservation of the initial geodesic ball without assuming iterate containment in advance. We further establish accelerated convergence rates for both geodesically convex and strongly geodesically convex objectives, without requiring restarts.

items.title: RapidDOC: Riccati-Preconditioned Implicit Differentiation for Differentiable Optimal Control under Operator Mismatch
items.summary: Differentiable optimal control embeds constrained optimization problems in data-driven pipelines by differentiating their optimality conditions and propagating task-loss gradients to model or objective parameters. A key observation is that forward optimization and backward sensitivity computation involve related stage-structured linear systems, making reuse of forward factorization information natural. However, direct reuse is generally invalid, because differences in linearization, barrier terms, regularization, and curvature can create a mismatch between the retained forward operator and the target operator defining the derivative. We therefore propose RapidDOC, a factorization-reuse method that leaves the target adjoint equation unchanged. The retained cache produces a candidate adjoint and, when its target residual exceeds the prescribed tolerance, serves as a fixed right preconditioner for GMRES. A cache-action error operator characterizes directional exactness, the preconditioned iteration, and the relation between target residual and outer-gradient error. An ablation on three constrained robotic OCPs shows that the proposed method achieves lower backward time than both target-system refactorization and a no-reuse iterative method, demonstrating the computational benefit of reusing the retained forward factorizations. Across open- and closed-loop parameter-learning experiments, the proposed method achieves learning performance comparable to the baselines, while yielding the lowest open-loop backward time on all three tasks and reducing total closed-loop solver-call time by 40.5-83.1% relative to the fastest competing method. Finally, deploying the learned controller on a physical vehicle reduces the median figure-eight tracking RMSE from 22.75 to 6.09 cm, demonstrating its potential for hardware deployment.

items.title: Sparse descent subspace-Newton thresholding algorithm for sparse optimization problems
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a sparse descent direction derived from the Newton direction within a low-dimensional subspace for sparse optimization problems. Building upon this direction and incorporating hard thresholding and orthogonal projection, we develop a novel algorithm termed the sparse descent subspace-Newton thresholding (SDSNT) algorithm. We further establish its global convergence under the restricted isometry property $δ_{3k}\leq \sqrt{3/20}$ of the measurement matrix. Numerical experiments on random sparse vector recovery and audio signal reconstruction reveal that SDSNT achieves comparable performance to several state-of-the-art algorithms. Notably, relative to most of them, it delivers superior recovery at high sparsity levels and improved efficiency at low sparsity levels.

items.title: Feature-preserving interface reconstruction using piecewise circles and cusps
items.summary: We present a geometric interface reconstruction method for Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) simulations that captures both curved interfaces and sharp features using only volume fraction data. We represent interfaces with linear facets, circular arcs, and corner facets formed by two lines or arcs joined within a single cell. We first propagate local orientation constraints through a graph and merge cells to resolve ambiguities, treating topological consistency as a first-class constraint. An optional conservative refinement improves $C^0$ continuity while preserving local volume constraints. Users can independently enable circular facets, corner facets, cell merging, and continuity refinement to balance accuracy and computational cost. In its simplest configuration, our method provides a fast local line-fitting scheme competitive with state-of-the-art PLIC methods. On standard static benchmarks, the full configuration reconstructs identifiable lines, circles, and sufficiently resolved corners to numerical precision on coarse, perturbed Cartesian meshes. On varying-curvature interfaces, it achieves third-order convergence in facet-gap error and approximately first-order convergence in curvature error. These results demonstrate global volume conservation and accurate reconstruction of curved and corner features.

items.title: Scaled-Gradient Hard Thresholding Algorithms for Sparse Signal Recovery
items.summary: Thresholding methods provide a simple iterative framework for sparse signal recovery by combining a search direction with a thresholding operation. Gradient-based search directions are computationally efficient because they require only first-order information for the error metric. We incorporate componentwise gradient scaling into this framework by preserving large-magnitude components and attenuating the remaining components of the gradient of error metric. Combining this strategy with hard thresholding yields scaled-gradient hard thresholding (SGHT) and its pursuit variant SGHTP. Under suitable restricted isometry conditions, we establish recovery error bounds for both methods that account for measurement noise and deviations from exact sparsity. Numerical experiments indicate that SGHTP achieves recovery performance comparable to established pursuit methods on the tested ECG signals.

items.title: Estimation of Quantum Umlaut Information
items.summary: Quantifying correlations is important for understanding how quantum states and channels support information processing. Quantum umlaut information $U$ connects such correlations to reliability in hypothesis testing and certain communication settings, but its known formulas require classical descriptions of the underlying states. To estimate correlations without these descriptions, we introduce measured quantum umlaut information $U^M$ by replacing Umegaki relative entropy with measured relative entropy. Its variational formulation leads to a quantum generative adversarial framework for estimating $U^M$ from measurement statistics of unknown bipartite states and classical-quantum channels. This framework optimizes reference states and measurements without reconstructing the target states or channel outputs. For classical-quantum channels, it also optimizes the input probabilities. We further analyze the relation between $U^M$ and $U$, deriving a state-dependent gap bound and characterizing equality for full-rank bipartite states. Numerical simulations show trained estimates close on average to independently computed numerical references for $U^M$ across the tested states and channels. These estimates could help assess how well quantum memories preserve correlations and how noise or drift affects input-output dependence in quantum transmitters and state-preparation devices.

items.title: POST-MIMO: Partition-Oriented Semantic Transmission for MIMO Point Cloud Delivery
items.summary: Point clouds have become a fundamental data format for emerging three dimensional (3D) applications, while their wireless delivery remains challenging due to the large data volume and irregular geometric structure. Existing semantic point cloud transmission methods are mainly developed for single-input single-output systems, making them difficult to apply directly to multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. To address this issue, we propose a partition-oriented semantic transmission framework for MIMO (POST-MIMO) point cloud delivery. POST-MIMO partitions the input point cloud into spatially coherent blocks and aligns them with parallel MIMO streams. Based on this block-aligned representation, the transmitter employs a hierarchical encoder to capture both intra-block local geometry and inter-block global dependency, while the auxiliary side information is transmitted jointly to assist reconstruction. At the receiver, a progressive decoder reconstructs the block geometry in a progressive manner and restores the final point cloud with block-aware adjustment. Experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and lower computational resource consumption than representative reference schemes under the considered MIMO setting.

items.title: Stochastic Mirror Descent under Dependent Observations
items.summary: We study the non-asymptotic convergence of Stochastic Mirror Descent (SMD) algorithm when the noisy first-order oracle is driven by dependent observations. Departing from the classical i.i.d. assumption underlying most existing guarantees, we introduce a flexible ``forgetting" condition that accommodates geometrically or polynomially dependent sequences. Under this condition we derive explicit finite-sample accuracy bounds for the averaged SMD iterates, recovering the classical $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates in the large- and small-initial-error regimes. We instantiate the general framework on two applications: high-dimensional linear regression with dependent regressors and nonparametric estimation of the drift function of a functional autoregressive model.

items.title: A Good-Vorticity Low-Regularity Integrator for the Inviscid Oldroyd--B System with Stress Diffusion
items.summary: We establish sharp convergence results for a sequential semi-implicit good-vorticity integrator for the two-dimensional inviscid Oldroyd--B system with stress diffusion on the torus. For exact solutions satisfying $u\in C_tB^{1+α}_{\infty,1}$ and $τ\in C_tB^α_{\infty,1}\cap L^1_tB^{2+α}_{\infty,1}$, $0\leα\le2$, we prove convergence in the critical norms $B^1_{\infty,1}\times B^0_{\infty,1}$, uniformly over the time nodes on every finite interval where these regularity assumptions hold, including the critical endpoint $α=0$. For $0<α\le2$, we obtain the rate $O(h^{α/2})$ without any additional time Hölder assumption, reaching first order at $α=2$. These algebraic exponents are optimal for this Eulerian scheme over the stated solution classes, as shown by fixed-data lower bounds in the case $a=b=0$ with nonzero velocity mean. For a fixed shear solution at critical regularity, we establish matching logarithmic upper and lower bounds on the numerical error, ruling out every positive algebraic convergence rate. We also prove that the gain of one stress derivative at the time nodes is optimal when the velocity is controlled in $B^1_{\infty,1}$, even for smooth initial stress.

items.title: DistFlow and Its Conic Relaxation: Regularity, Monotonicity, and Hybrid Exactness via Graph Decomposition
items.summary: Classical exactness conditions for conic relaxations of the DistFlow model rely, among other assumptions, either on all nodal injections being adjustable or on a network-wide path condition. In practice, these conditions may not hold uniformly across a feeder: controllable distributed energy resources (DERs) sit at some buses and fixed loads at others, while reverse flows from DER-rich regions can violate the path condition. This paper certifies exactness region by region and composes the regional certificates, accounting for perturbations that propagate downstream through voltages. We first introduce a subtree voltage stability region, in which the network and all compatible subtrees remain regular. Within it, two endpoint sign conditions, one relaxing the nonnegative-flow assumption and one implied by the classical path condition, yield monotone responses of voltages, currents, and losses to root voltages. Using duality, the implicit function theorem, and sign properties of inverse sensitivity matrices, we recast both classical arguments as individual sign certificates on branch multipliers. This turns exactness into a branchwise property that can be certified region by region. A partition rule then splits the network into dispatchable and passive subtrees, and a hybrid certificate combines their local conditions into exactness of the full-network relaxation, under additional operating-limit and objective conditions. In particular, placing controllable DERs at both ends of a branch with large reverse flow exempts that branch from the passive sign conditions.

items.title: Algebraic Vector Fields of Connected Semi-simple Matrix Groups are 3-generated
items.summary: We show that the Lie algebra of algebraic vector fields for any connected, semi-simple matrix group over $\mathbb{F}$, for $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}$, can be generated by three $\mathbb{F}$-complete algebraic vector fields.

items.title: Multiple Swap Local Search Approximations for Uniform-Cost Capacitated Facility Location with Extensions to Outliers
items.summary: We study metric facility location with customer incompatibilities, where the clients assigned to each facility must satisfy prescribed independence constraints. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$. We develop a polynomial-time \((1+\sqrt{2}+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for this setting. We further obtain a polynomial-time \((15+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for the case of non-uniform facility-opening costs when $\mathcal M$ is a partition matroid that only permits $b_g$ clients to be assigned to a facility for each group $g$ in the partition. Both settings are substantial generalizations of Capacitated Facility Location with uniform capacities. Our algorithms are based on local search using add, delete, and single-swap operations. As with CFL, bounding the connection cost is reasonably straightforward using supermodularity of the minimum connection-cost function. However, bounding the facility opening costs requires novel arguments in both cases. We use a ``compression'' argument based on matroid exchange principles to identify a subset of the locally opened facilities whose size is no larger than that of an optimal facility set. The opening costs of facilities outside this subset can be bounded using supermodularity, while bounding the costs of the remaining facilities requires different arguments. It is natural to consider a variant where each possible facility $i$ has its own matroid $\mathcal M_i$ defining the subsets of clients it can feasibly serve. We also show problem is at least as hard to approximate as Set Cover even if all $\mathcal M_i$ are partition matroids that have the same partition of clients, just different group bounds $b_g$.

items.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
items.summary: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$. Lean checks the algebraic certificate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family implementations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths $n=13,15$, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.

items.title: General Frequency Principle for Linear Approximation Classes
items.summary: In this paper, we study a general frequency principle under gradient descent training for the finite linear approximation classes. Under suitable assumptions, we prove that the learner amplitude relative to the target amplitude vanishes at high frequencies, uniformly throughout training. We also establish sufficient conditions for low-frequency priority, covering single-frequency targets trained separately and two frequency components trained in the same run. This general frequency principle does not imply that lower frequencies always converge faster. Instead, for two frequencies that satisfy certain comparison conditions, one component will take longer to learn than the other; and in common cases, the longer component has higher frequency. Numerical experiments with Legendre and trigonometric bases validate the theoretical results.

items.title: Traveling Salesman Problem on Graphs with Proportional Independent Set
items.summary: We give a deterministic algorithm for minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in undirected graphs with arbitrary real edge costs and an independent set of size at least $αn$, for any fixed $3/7<α\le1/2$. It runs in $O^*(γ(α)^n)$ time for an explicit constant $γ(α)<2$; for bipartite graphs, the bound is $O^*((1+2\sqrt2)^{n/2})\approx O^*(1.957^n)$. The algorithm is based on a restricted Held--Karp dynamic program. Its state enumeration uses structural properties of minimum-cost assignments arising from a regular triangulation of a product of simplices.

items.title: Koopman--Lyapunov and Koopman--Riccati Controller Synthesis
items.summary: While the Koopman operator-based lifted representations of nonlinear autonomous and controlled systems have been well covered in the literature, the direct controller synthesis problem largely remains open. As the controlled system is generally a bilinear (instead of fully linear) Koopman model, controller synthesis appears to lose the linear--quadratic structures of the classical Lyapunov and Riccati methods for finite-dimensional linear systems. However, in infinite dimensions, bilinearity in the feature map should be merely artifactual and hence reducible to linearity in principle. In this work, by considering the operator semigroups in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space with a linear--Sobolev kernel and utilizing the Yosida approximation of their generators, the synthesis problems of a stabilizing controller and an input-unconstrained optimal controller can be formulated as an operator Lyapunov inequality and an operator Riccati equation, respectively. These formulations recover the desirable linear--quadratic structures, and hence, with sample data, they are solvable efficiently in analogous ways to usual linear systems by semidefinite programming solvers and Kleinman iterations, respectively. In addition to proving control performance bounds dependent on the sampling denseness and Yosida regularization, through numerical comparison to linearized LQR, bilinear EDMD-based synthesis, nonlinear MPC, and Koopman MPC methods on numerical models and process control examples, this work demonstrates the proposed Koopman--Riccati synthesis as a computationally efficient approach to obtain a near-optimal state-feedback control law.

items.title: The Competitive Ratio of Online Budgeted Allocation is Strictly Smaller than $1-1/e$
items.summary: A well-known conjecture in online algorithms is that the (randomized) competitive ratio of online budgeted allocation is $1-1/e$. We refute this conjecture and show that every randomized online algorithm has competitive ratio at most $1 - 1/e - \varepsilon$ for a (small) absolute constant $\varepsilon > 0$.

items.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
items.summary: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

items.title: Local Budget Benefits, Population Commitment, and Solver Performance: A DGO Case Study with Controlled DE Transfer
items.summary: An evaluated candidate can improve a local search step, alter the population used by later steps, and affect a solver's final result. We distinguish these three questions using Da Gou Gun Optimization (DGO), a population optimizer designed for this study. Its JQ100 configuration evaluates an interpolation candidate during a two-sided probe. We define local budget value, population commitment effects and complete-policy performance, and give an exact example in which a locally better commitment leads to a worse continuation. Short-horizon matched comparisons favor interpolation on eligible quadratic states. Paired continuations yield mixed effect estimates, with primary group intervals spanning zero. Complete-policy comparisons favor JQ100 over the tested classical references in aggregate; a matched-start comparison has favorable means but intervals spanning parity. On 24 boxed BBOB functions, target-truncated geometric-mean error ratios favor JQ100 over the tested classical policies and favor L-SHADE and CMA-ES over JQ100 under the stated initialization and stopping rules. Local evaluation gains, commitment effects and solver competitiveness therefore require separate comparisons.

items.title: Robust edge multiscale space based hybrid Schwarz preconditioner for high-frequency Helmholtz problems
items.summary: We develop a novel hybrid Schwarz method, termed the robust edge multiscale space based hybrid Schwarz method (REMs-HS), for the efficient solution of high-frequency Helmholtz problems. The method combines a one-level restricted additive Schwarz preconditioner with impedance transmission conditions (RAS-imp) and an edge multiscale (EMs) coarse solver in a multiplicative way. A key ingredient of our construction is a modified impedance boundary condition (mIBC), which is imposed both on the subdomain problems and on the local problems that generate the EMs coarse space. Compared with the original impedance boundary condition, the mIBC makes the proposed method both stable and inexpensive theoretically. We prove that the resulting REMs-HS preconditioner gives rise to a uniform convergent fixed-point iteration for large wavenumbers. Moreover, the required resolution conditions are substantially relaxed. Only a mild condition on the level parameter $\ell$ of the hierarchical coarse basis $\ell>\frac{1}{2}\log_2 k$ is needed, which is markedly weaker than the conditions in previous analyses. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the robustness of the proposed method for Helmholtz problems with large wavenumbers.

items.title: Stochastic and Noisy Oracles in Smooth Continuous Optimization
items.summary: We review models of inexact computational oracles in smooth continuous optimization and their implications for the convergence, computational complexity, and attainable accuracy of optimization algorithms. We adopt a framework in which zeroth-,first-, and second-order oracles are characterized by quantitative error bounds and may accept additional control parameters that influence both their accuracy and computational cost. We introduce deterministic and stochastic oracle models and illustrate their properties through a variety of examples, including finite-difference approximations, stochastic gradients, and randomized derivative estimators. Particular attention is given to the distinction between absolute and relative errors, bias and variance, and stochastic function evaluations with independent or coupled randomness. A central theme of the review is the use of common analytical tools to recover and compare convergence and complexity guarantees under different oracle models. For deterministic and stochastic first-order methods, we show how a general descent inequality leads to complexity bounds under various assumptions on the objective function and all proposed oracle models. In the stochastic setting, we develop bounds on expected stopping times and the accuracy that can be guaranteed under different oracle conditions. We also examine the total computational complexity of algorithms relying on specific oracle constructions and briefly review models of inexact second- order information and their use in optimization algorithms.

items.title: Approximate Bayesian Fusion
items.summary: Distributed inference plays an important role in modern computational statistics and machine learning. In the frequentist setting, methods can often aggregate results by simply averaging estimators computed on data subsets. However, distributed Bayesian inference is more challenging, as it requires reconstructing the full posterior by combining subposterior distributions computed on different machines. Bayesian Fusion performs distributed Bayesian inference exactly, but at a sizeable computational cost. We propose a method that uses numerical approximations to reduce the cost of the most computationally expensive steps of Bayesian Fusion, and expands its domain of applicability. We bound the numerical error as a function of the step size of the approximation. Under regularity conditions, our approach can approximate the target posterior distribution to an arbitrary degree of accuracy, and is a practical and efficient alternative for large-scale distributed Bayesian inference. In numerical experiments on a logistic regression with more than $300{,}000$ observations, our method reaches the accuracy reported for Divide-and-Conquer Bayesian Fusion about two orders of magnitude faster. On a proportional hazards model with non-Gaussian posteriors, which lacks the lower bounds that Bayesian Fusion requires, our method reproduces funnel features of the posterior that simpler methods like Consensus Monte Carlo miss.

items.title: Stochastic Linesearch Methods for Stochastic Variational Inequality Problems: Parameter-Free Schemes and Non-Monotone Variants
items.summary: Much of the existing convergence guarantees and rate statements for stochastic variational inequality (SVI) problems are limited to stochastic approximation schemes that employ constant or diminishing steplength sequences bounded by some reciprocal of the Lipschitz constant $L$ of the map. This requires both knowing such constants and may lead to debilitatingly small steplengths, afflicting the scheme with potentially poor performance. We propose a parameter-free stochastic extragradient method with periodically restarted linesearch (\textbf{SEG-LS}) for solving pseudomonotone and monotone SVI problems. The resulting stepsize sequence is neither monotone nor requires prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant $L$. We show that the iteration and sample complexities for computing a point whose residual has norm at most $ε$ in expectation are $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$, respectively. These results improve to $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-1})$ and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ in the monotone setting. In addition, we propose a periodically restarted biased stochastic linesearch method (\textbf{B-SLAM}) for solving non-monotone SVIs under strict copositivity. The resulting iteration and sample complexities are $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$, respectively. Preliminary numerics support these findings and display promise.

items.title: String-averaging bargaining in solidarity cooperative games
items.summary: We consider the situation that the grand set of all players, in a cooperative game in characteristic function form with a nonempty core, consists of recognizable subsets of players. The underlying assumption is that the players of each subset have something in common between themselves which is not shared by the players of other subsets. For example, the members of these subsets are distinguishable by their nationalities or by their geographic locations or by some other market-related economic or social property. In addition to the agreement of all players to play the game to reach a point in the core, the members of each subset want to steer the iterative orbit of the bargaining process to a point in the core that will reflect the strength of their solidarity within their subset. This is why we call such subsets solidarity sets. The solidarity means that players of a solidarity set are willing to participate in coalitions that include only members of their solidarity set and are not willing to participate in coalitions of other solidarity sets. The question is how can such a game be played? Is there an iterative bargaining scheme that will generate a sequence of payoffs that converges to a point in the core which reflects the solidarity of the members of the solidarity sets? We propose bargaining schemes that allow the members of each solidarity set to perform, independently from other solidarity sets and, therefore, simultaneously in time, a full but finite sweep of intercoalitional collaboration. Then the end-points of all these sweeps are combined into a single payoff vector via a convex combination wherein the coefficients of the convex combination may reflect some a priori knowledge about the relative strengths of the different solidarity sets. These bargaining schemes are applied to a new type of cooperative game that we call solidarity cooperative game (SCG).

items.title: Box-Cone Representations of Bound-Factor RLT Constraints in Semidefinite Relaxations
items.summary: Linear inequalities can generate large constraint systems in semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs, making the quadratic subproblems of splitting methods expensive to solve. We develop a box-cone representation of bound-factor reformulation-linearization technique (RLT) constraints in semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs. These constraints arise by multiplying each original linear inequality by every binary variable and its complement and linearizing the resulting products. Our key observation is that all products generated by one inequality share a common slack and admit an exact representation in the standard cone over the unit box. This box-cone representation processes the inequalities through independent explicit projections, without introducing a separate nonnegative slack for each scalar RLT inequality. We illustrate the computational use of the representation within standard two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The resulting subproblems require linear solves with a reusable factorization and explicit cone projections, without enlarging the semidefinite matrix. Experiments on 257 binary quadratic programs compare this implementation with SDPNAL+. A second application groups Max-Cut triangle inequalities into box cones and uses the resulting bounds within an existing branch-and-bound framework. Tests on 220 graphs show competitive performance with MADAM using only triangle cuts. Together, these applications illustrate the representation's usefulness as a building block for first-order methods.

items.title: Faster #PPM from faster #3SAT
items.summary: The counting variant (#PPM) of the permutation pattern matching (PPM) problem asks for the number of occurrences of a permutation pattern in a host permutation of length $n$. The problem admits faster algorithms than the trivial $O^*(2^n)$ time enumeration; the best known running time, for both PPM and #PPM, is $O(1.415^n)$ (Gawrychowski and Rzepecki). It is also known that PPM is ETH-hard: an algorithm with running time $2^{o(n/\log{n})}$ would imply a subexponential algorithm for 3SAT (Jelínek, Opler, and Pekárek). We give a reduction in the opposite direction, showing that an algorithm for counting satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF formula (#3SAT) in time $2^{O({n}/{f(n)})}$, where $n$ is the number of variables, yields an algorithm for #PPM with running time $2^{O({n \sqrt{\log{f(n)}/{f(n)}}})}$. In particular, the recently claimed refutation of ETH by OpenAI implies a #3SAT algorithm with an improvement factor $f(n) \in Ω(\sqrt{\log{n}}/\log\log{n})$ in the exponent; this yields, through our reduction, a subexponential algorithm for #PPM.

items.title: Meshless Latent Dynamics Models for Model Order Reduction of time-dependent Partial Differential Equations
items.summary: Latent dynamics learning has emerged as a prominent approach for Model Order Reduction (MOR) of time-dependent, parameterized Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Traditional autoencoder-based approaches are intrinsically tied to fixed spatial discretizations during both training and inference, motivating the development of meshless methodologies. In this context, conditioning provides a natural mechanism for representing temporal evolution through spatially continuous functions, enabling mesh-agnostic Latent Dynamics Models (LDMs). In this work, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for mesh-agnostic LDMs based on conditioning in Neural Fields (NeFs). Leveraging a taxonomy of conditioning mechanisms (weak, strong, and pure), we formulate meshless LDMs as NeFs conditioned on a latent state. We establish a Universal Approximation Theorem (UAT) for this class of models and analyze their stability by deriving Lipschitz bounds for different conditioning mechanisms. Our analysis reveals an expressivity--stability trade-off, providing insight into why more expressive conditioning, despite its higher representational capacity, can potentially degrade performance during temporal extrapolation. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of meshless and mesh-based architectures in the continuous limit of the spatial discretization, showing that meshless models guarantee grid-independent Lipschitz bounds, unlike mesh-based counterparts. Our experiments across Burgers' equation, Navier--Stokes flow past a cylinder, and linear advection show that meshless LDMs can achieve predictive accuracy comparable to or better than their mesh-based counterparts while using only 2% of the trainable parameters and exhibiting nearly constant error across spatial discretizations.

items.title: When can Optimally Trained Transformers Achieve Near-Lossless Token Prediction for non-Markovian Data?
items.summary: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $α^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $α$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.

items.title: Privacy-Constrained Function Computation in Distributed Databases
items.summary: Consider distributed databases that contain both sensitive (private) and non-sensitive (public) attributes. A user seeks to compute a function of public attributes and side information by interacting with the databases and downloading their responses. In this paper, we study the trade-offs among download cost, information leakage about the private attributes, and distortion between the computed function and its reconstruction, referred to as the capacity region. Our main contributions are as follows. For a single database, we provide a complete characterization of the capacity region for general discrete sources and characterize the capacity region of two different setups for Gaussian sources when the computed function is defined as the sum of the public attribute and side information. For distributed databases, we establish inner and outer bounds on the capacity region of discrete sources and we characterize the capacity region when the databases and the side information are mutually independent. As a special instance, we study lossless function computation, and results analogous to the lossy case are obtained.

items.title: Omniprediction for All Mixable Proper Losses and Beyond
items.summary: Omniprediction concerns the task of making predictions that are simultaneously accurate with respect to different losses. Earlier results by [CV09] show that in an online learning setting, $O(\log(|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{L}|))$ regret is achievable simultaneously against every predictor in a finite predictor class $\mathcal{F}$ and for every loss in a finite class $\mathcal{L}$ of mixable proper losses, while recent advances [OKK25, FP26] show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T\log(|\mathcal{F}||\mathcal{L}|)})$ regret is achievable simultaneously for every loss in a finite class $\mathcal{L}$ of bounded losses. In this work, we ask whether sublinear regret remains possible when $\mathcal{L}$ is an infinite class of proper losses. Our first result gives a negative answer in general: even when $\mathcal{F}$ contains only two linear predictors, it is impossible to achieve sublinear regret simultaneously for all bounded proper losses. We then show that $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}(\log|\mathcal{F}|)^{2/3})$ regret is achievable simultaneously for \textit{all} mixable proper losses and that this bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors. This optimal rate stands in stark contrast to the constant (in $T$) regret achievable for a finite class of mixable proper losses. Finally, we extend our algorithm to obtain a best-of-all-worlds result: in addition to the new regret guarantee for all mixable proper losses, the resulting algorithm simultaneously achieves the existing guarantees for finite loss classes. With appropriate choices of these finite classes, our algorithm simultaneously achieves constant regret for squared loss and log loss, $\widetilde{O}(T^{1/3}(\log|\mathcal{F}|)^{2/3})$ regret for all mixable proper losses, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{F}|})$ regret for $0$-$1$ loss, all Lipschitz losses, all GLM losses, and other structured families.

items.title: CuPIQP: A Batched and Differentiable QP Solver on GPUs for Robot Learning and Control
items.summary: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present \textsc{cuPIQP}, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau} and $4.26\times$ over eight-core \textsc{PIQP}. In an end-to-end learning task, \textsc{cuPIQP} accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over \textsc{QPAX} and $7.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau}. By reducing the computational cost, \textsc{cuPIQP} provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.

items.title: Neural Network Methods in the 2BSDE Formalism for Solving the High-Dimensional Black--Scholes Equation with Transaction Costs
items.summary: A 2BSDE system is written down for a $(D+1)$-dimensional Black--Scholes partial differential equation (PDE) with the Leland transaction cost model which incorporates the sign of the curvature. The 2BSDE system takes input from the ``speed'' (derivative of the curvature). This system is solved using a single ResNet neural network which learns both the solution to the PDE as well as the degrees of freedom in the curvature matrix. The network is used to learn the price of derivatives such as call options and butterfly spreads on geometric baskets for $D=10,100$ achieving a time-averaged RMSE of less than $0.1$ in each case.

items.title: Kernel-based Interpolatory Methods for Context Compression of Attention Mechanisms
items.summary: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.

items.title: Hypergraph cycle enumeration for efficient inference of planted k-XOR with smooth trade-off
items.summary: We introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems. We study HCE on one representative problem from this class, namely planted noisy k-XOR, also known as sparse Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). Both theoretically and empirically, HCE achieves comparable recovery behavior to Kikuchi method, matching Kikuchi hierarchy. We identify parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi method, showing that neither algorithm is universally better. We also show a subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE by replacing one of the algorithm's steps with a quantum walk. Our classical and quantum algorithms do not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for the practically relevant regime of large size and high noise strength.

items.title: Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
items.summary: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

items.title: Fast and Accurate Hydro Unit Commitment
items.summary: We introduce a fast novel algorithm to commit hydro-generators. We show that our algorithm can commit 56 generators for 200 days 10,000 times faster than Hexaly, the leading commercial solver for scheduling problems, without sacrificing solution quality. Our method can commit 1792 generators for an entire year in approximately 20 seconds on commodity hardware. Hexaly is unable to solve problems of this size in reasonable time. We attain this runtime improvement by introducing a greedy-heuristic tailored for hydro units. We provide a direction for a possible proof that the error our solver makes decreases with the problem size. This is supported by our experimental results. We prove that our solver's runtime scales log-linearly in the number of generators and time periods.

items.title: Simple Cuts, Simple Landscape: Dimension-Free Rank Bounds for Burer-Monteiro Factorizations via Rank-Width
items.summary: In this work, we study Burer-Monteiro factorizations of semidefinite programs with unit diagonal constraints. For a real symmetric cost matrix whose rank-width over $\mathbb{R}$ is at most $k$, we prove that every non-flat second-order stationary point of the factorized problem is globally optimal whenever the factorization rank is at least $2k$, independently of the matrix size.

items.title: Stochastic Minimum Spanning Tree Identification with Binary Weights
items.summary: We introduce the Stochastic MST Identification Problem, with binary weights. In this problem, we need to identify a minimum spanning tree (MST) of a graph, each of whose edge weights is either 0 or 1. The weight of each edge $e$ is a random variable which is 1 with probability $p_e$ and 0 with probability $1-p_e$. The probability $p_e$ is given for each edge $e$, but the realized weight of an edge can only be determined by querying the edge. The problem is then to determine a strategy for querying the edges of the graph that minimizes the expected number of queries that need to be performed until we can identify a subset of edges that form an MST of the graph. We address both adaptive and non-adaptive versions of this problem. For the non-adaptive version of our Stochastic MST Identification problem, we give an $O(\log E)$-approximation algorithm via a reduction to submodular ranking. For the adaptive version, we show that solving the problem is trivial when all $p_e$ are equal to 1/2, because of a relation to the Tutte polynomial. However, computing the expected cost of an optimal querying strategy is #P-hard, even when all $p_e$ equal $\frac{1}{2}$. For arbitrary $p_e$ values, we present a constant-factor approximation algorithm for simple planar graphs. We investigate the question of whether the submodular goal value approach of Deshpande et al. could be used to achieve a $\log$-factor approximation algorithm that would work for arbitrary $p_e$ values and general graphs. In this context, we address the structural question of determining optimal submodular goal values for MST identification in graphs.

items.title: The nodally bound-preserving finite element method for the transport equation
items.summary: Numerical approximations of transport problems, even when stabilised, often violate the bounds respected by the exact solution. Depending on the problem being solved, this can produce non-physical results, such as negative densities or higher-than-unity concentrations. Various bound-preserving numerical methods exist, yet they are usually either conditionally stable or only first-order accurate. In this context, the present work extends the nodally bound-preserving finite element method to the linear transport equation. As a baseline discretisation we use the least-squares finite element method, which is instrumental in achieving unconditional stability for second-order time stepping. It also leads to symmetric algebraic systems, thereby enabling simple, efficient solvers, which we further enhance through Anderson acceleration. Unconditional stability is proved for the backward Euler and Crank--Nicolson discretisations. We also derive error estimates for the fully discrete second-order scheme and provide various numerical examples, including two-phase incompressible flows.

items.title: Tight Lower Bounds for Distributional Paging
items.summary: Distributional paging seeks a polynomial-time eviction rule that competes with the optimal \emph{online} policy $\mathrm{OPT}$ when requests come from a known stochastic source. Two algorithms by Lund, Phillips, and Reingold [FOCS, 1994] are canonical. Their randomized \emph{dominating distribution} algorithm, for Markov sources, evicts a page drawn from a distribution over the cache satisfying pairwise linear inequalities; their deterministic \emph{median} algorithm, for sources with independent inter-arrival times across pages, evicts the cached page with the largest lower median of its conditional next-request time. Their original guarantees of $4$ and $5$ were recently improved to $2$ and $4$ by Pabbaraju and Vakilian [ICALP 2025]. We show that neither improved constant can be reduced in its respective source model. For Markov paging, we give two complementary factor-$2$ lower-bound constructions, each with an explicit polynomial-time dominating selector. A directed-cycle family has ratio $2k/(k+1)$, while a recurrent four-page family with cache size three has ratio $2-4\varepsilon/3$. For the independent inter-arrival model, we show that the median algorithm is not $c$-competitive for any $c<4$. These are separate results for distinct stochastic models. Matching the known upper bounds, they establish tight competitive ratios of $2$ and $4$, respectively, improving on previous lower bounds of $1.5907$ and $1.511$.

items.title: Capacitated Clustering with Few Extra Centers
items.summary: In capacitated $(k,z)$-clustering, we open $k$ centers and assign every client to a center within its capacity, minimizing the sum of $z$-th powers of the distances; $k$-median and $k$-means are the cases $z=1$ and $z=2$. We study polynomial-time algorithms that open $k+\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ centers but respect the capacities exactly. All ratios hold up to an additive $δ$ for every fixed $δ>0$. For uniform soft capacities in low dimensions, we obtain ratio $β-(β-1)\varepsilon$, where $β=3^z$ if the clients or the locations have bounded doubling dimension, and $β=\mathcal{B}_z<3^z$ for $z>1$ if the clients do and centers may lie anywhere in $\mathbb{R}^d$. This gives $3-2\varepsilon$ for $k$-median and $5-4\varepsilon$ for Euclidean $k$-means. We also obtain ratios bounded by a constant for hard capacities, and $1+(3^z-1)e^{-\varepsilon}$ for non-uniform soft capacities. These are the first polynomial-time ratios with $(1+\varepsilon)k$ centers that are bounded by a constant, apart from uniform $k$-median in the plane. For uniform $k$-median in general metrics, we obtain $3+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)$ with soft and $7+2\ln(1/\varepsilon)$ with hard capacities, improving the previous $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$. Splitting the clusters of a near-optimal uncapacitated solution into groups of at most $U$ clients, where $U$ is the capacity, gives fewer than $2k$ groups. With fewer centers, groups must share centers. Each extra center gives private centers to about two groups, since a center of an optimal solution that serves only such groups can be closed. Thus $\lfloor\varepsilon k\rfloor$ extra centers remove almost an $\varepsilon$-fraction of the extra cost caused by sharing.

items.title: Improved Gradient Complexity for Quasi-Newton Proximal Extragradient Methods via Certified Curvature Reuse
items.summary: We study how curvature estimated from gradient differences can accelerate proximal-extragradient quasi-Newton methods. Existing global guarantees for QNPE, A-QNPE, and OL-OQN learn Hessian approximations online and incur dimension dependence through regret bounds. We introduce certified curvature reuse: one finite-difference probe per iteration refreshes a group of Hessian columns, while a path-length certificate controls the error of stale columns and determines the step. Each iteration uses at most three gradient queries and one regularized linear solve (or trust-region step), without a gradient line search or an inner oracle-querying loop. In the convex and strongly convex settings, bisection on stored scalar quantities selects a near-maximal certified stepsize; in the nonconvex setting, a uniform certificate gives an explicit learning rate. With other problem parameters fixed, the convex method attains $O(\min\{k^{-2},dk^{-3}\})$ in a single run, with no logarithmic factor or additive dimension term, matching accelerated gradient descent (AGD) for $k\lesssim d$ and improving on A-QNPE thereafter. In the strongly convex setting with condition number $κ$, a single run matches AGD's $(1-Θ(κ^{-1/2}))^k$ rate for $k\lesssim d\logκ$ and achieves a superlinear upper envelope, eventually scaling as $(1+k^2/B^2)^{-k}$ with $B=\tilde O(dκ)$, improving on QNPE. In the nonconvex setting, the method finds an $\varepsilon$-stationary point in $O(\min\{d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-3/2},\varepsilon^{-7/4}\})$ gradient queries, improving on OL-OQN's $O(d^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-13/8})$. For sparse Hessians, $d$ is replaced by an effective dimension $χ\le d$. We also compare our bounds with lazy-Hessian, double-loop, and cutting-plane methods.

items.title: On Zeros and Algorithms for Disordered Systems II: The Antiferromagnetic Ising Model up to Kesten-Stigum
items.summary: We give the first polynomial-time algorithm to estimate the partition function of the antiferromagnetic Ising model on the uniformly random $d$-regular graph to arbitrarily high accuracy for all inverse temperatures up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold. This is the entire regime in which the model is "replica symmetric," and is conjectured to be optimal for polynomial-time counting and sampling. To achieve our algorithmic result, we establish the absence of Fisher zeros for the partition function in a constant-width strip around the interval from $0$ up to the Kesten-Stigum threshold, with high probability over the randomness of the input graph. AI Disclosure: The overarching vision and proof architecture were developed solely by the authors without AI input. GPT 5.5 Pro was used, with extensive guidance from the authors, for only a few minor technical aspects of the proof. The authors independently verified correctness and wrote everything by hand. We take full responsibility for its contents. A more detailed statement can be found in Section 1.2.

items.title: Approximating Minimum Spanning Trees in Metrics under Semi-Random Corruptions
items.summary: We study the problem of finding minimum spanning trees in semi-random corrupted metrics. In this problem proposed by Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), we start with a metric space $\mathcal{M} = (X, d)$. The adversary independently corrupts each pairwise distance with probability $p$. The algorithm only observes these possibly corrupted distances and must output a spanning tree whose expected cost (in the true metric) is multiplicatively close to the minimum spanning tree cost. Prior work showed that losing a factor of $Ω(\log n)$ is necessary, even if the algorithm may adaptively select $O(n/\log n)$ points and probe the true distances between them. However, no upper bounds were known. We study three regimes based on whether the adversary can only increase, decrease, or arbitrarily change the corrupted distances. We show the following: (1) In the increase-only setting, we give a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. (2) In the decrease-only setting, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. Additionally, we show an $O(\log^4 n)$-approximation algorithm that runs in quasi-polynomial time $n^{O(\log n)}$, for any constant $p \leq 0.1$. Moreover, we show that a polynomial-time algorithm computing an $n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$-approximation is unlikely to exist. (3) In the general setting, where the adversary can both increase and decrease distances, we show an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for every $0 \leq p < \frac{1}{4}$. Further, we show that no $o(n)$-approximation is possible for $\frac{1}{2} \leq p < 1$. Our algorithms answer the main open question in Bateni et al.'s work; moreover, the $O(\log n)$-approximations in the latter two settings are information-theoretically optimal.

items.title: Maximum Cardinality Matching in $n^{2+o(1)}$ Time
items.summary: We consider the maximum cardinality matching problem in general graphs, and give an $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm for the problem. Our work builds on recent work on combinatorial algorithms for maximum flow and extends the techniques to skew-symmetric flow problems which capture general matchings as a special case.

items.title: When Imputation Changes the Nearest Neighbor: Exact Certification of Similarity Retrieval for Incomplete Sensor Time Series
items.summary: Sensor time series routinely reach similarity search with missing values, and the retrieved neighbours then depend on how the gaps were filled. We ask which retrieval conclusions hold for every admissible completion of an incomplete query. For a family of window-minimum distances that contains the $L_1$ distance as its separable end we give a pairwise certificate that one candidate is strictly closer than another, a guaranteed candidate set that contains every possible nearest neighbour, and a certificate that a nearest-neighbour label cannot change. The guarantees hold uniformly over the specified box and apply to the true query whenever it lies inside. At the separable end a closed form is known, but beyond it the worst-case gap need not be attained at a corner of the box. We prove a finite reduction to critical values, give an exact interval dynamic programme for the worst-case ranking gap, and a quadratic-time fast layer of valid bounds and feasible witnesses, supported by an exact criterion for when the feature-box relaxation is tight. On three traffic-sensor collections with real gap patterns, linear interpolation changes the nearest neighbour in 15 to 33 percent of the queries. At the full band the feature-box relaxation misses up to 14 percent of the exactly stable boundary pairs, whereas fixed-completion and Monte Carlo checks issue false certificates. The fast layer resolves about 90 percent of all tested boundary pairs without dynamic programming, and on paired network-scale queries the exact method is 82 to 110 times faster than the programme alone. Label certificates transfer to three public benchmarks, and the band width trades forecasting accuracy and certification coverage for lower imputation sensitivity, with dataset-dependent crossovers.

items.title: The Tight Competitive Ratio of Greedy for Online Steiner Forest
items.summary: The online Steiner Forest problem is a fundamental network design problem in which terminal pairs arrive one at a time and an algorithm must irrevocably purchase edges connecting each pair. The natural greedy algorithm connects each terminal pair by a shortest path after making all previously purchased edges free. Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal (SODA 1996) proved that this algorithm is $O(log^2 k)$-competitive and conjectured an $O(log k)$ bound, where $k$ is the number of terminal pairs. Bamas, Drygala, and Maggiori (SODA 2022) obtained an $O(\log \NumPairs\log\log \NumPairs)$ bound for greedy on a restricted class of inputs, leaving the general case open. In this paper, we resolve the competitive ratio of the greedy algorithm for online Steiner Forest, proving that it is tightly $Θ(log(k) log log(k))$. Specifically, we establish an $O(log(k) log log(k))$ upper bound for arbitrary instances and construct a matching $Ω(log(k) log log(k))$ lower bound. Our results refute the $O(log k)$ conjecture of Awerbuch, Azar, and Bartal and establish a tight $Θ(log log k)$ separation between the greedy algorithm and the best possible online algorithm for Steiner Forest.

items.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
items.summary: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-\textsf{Majority}, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-\textsf{Majority} achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-\textsf{Majority} that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.

items.title: Exact Competitive Ratios of Index Rules for Scheduling with Obligatory Testing
items.summary: We revisit scheduling with obligatory testing, where each job consists of two operations: a test with an initially known time and an operation whose processing time is revealed upon completion of the job's test. We develop an iterative competitive-ratio-preserving instance-reduction method that enables us to compute exact competitive ratios directly on highly structured instances for various index rules. Our main result is a clean analysis showing that the competitive ratio of the algorithm $1$-SORT is exactly the Golden Ratio $\varphi\approx 1.618$, improving the recent best-known upper bound of $1.861$ for arbitrary testing times. We further leverage this method to obtain near-tight bounds for a simple randomized algorithm on instances with uniform testing times.

items.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
items.summary: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

items.title: A Behavioral approach to Constrained Linear Quadratic Control: Feasibility and Optimality
items.summary: This paper develops a constrained linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control framework within the behavioral approach. Unlike classical formulations that rely on state-input representations, our method treats both the system dynamics and the constraints as trajectory-level objects. The system is modeled through a kernel representation, while inequality constraints are captured using behavioral inequalities defined over infinite-dimensional convex cones. Using quadratic differential forms (QDFs) to encode performance indices, we formulate the constrained LQ problem as a convex variational optimization over trajectories. By employing Gateaux differentials, we derive the stationarity and complementarity conditions and show that they admit a representation as an augmented behavioral system whose unique decomposition into autonomous and controllable sub-behaviors yields a complete parameterization of all optimal constrained trajectories. The resulting conditions constitute a behavioral analogue of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) framework. A numerical example illustrates the effect of inequality constraints on the optimal behavior. The framework provides a general, trajectory-level representation for constrained optimal control and opens avenues for closed-loop and data-driven extensions.

items.title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
items.summary: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $σ=αμ+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at https://github.com/ShwStone/DecodingPredict.

items.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
items.summary: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

items.title: Single-Temperature Ranked Greedy Cluster Exchange for Max-Cut on Two-Dimensional Tori
items.summary: Ground-state search in two-dimensional Ising spin glasses on large toroidal lattices remains challenging for local-update heuristics because rugged energy barriers impede relaxation across metastable states. Equivalent to zero-field toroidal Max-Cut problems, these spin-glass instances also serve as standard benchmarks for optimization heuristics. Many Monte Carlo approaches combine single-spin flips or cluster moves with temperature ladders or annealing schedules, yet even with tuned parameters, rarely achieve rapid, reliable ground-state convergence at scale. Here, we address the need for faster ground-state search through cooperation between replicas. We introduce ranked greedy cluster exchange (RGCX) and combine it with fixed-temperature Metropolis sweeps to form single-temperature RGCX. Replicas are ranked by cut to determine the pair-processing order. Each pair deterministically exchanges every disagreement cluster that raises the better replica's cut, retaining the complement and conserving the pair's summed cut. On the 20,000-spin Gset instance G81, the estimated runtime to reach the certified optimum with 99% success probability (TTS99) was 12.1 s on an 8-core desktop computer. With the same population size, exchange interval and temperature, the method reached the best known cuts on all 17 toroidal Gset graphs, including 9 certified optima. These findings advance ground-state search on large two-dimensional tori by establishing single-temperature RGCX as an efficient population-based method that combines ranked greedy cluster exchange with fixed-temperature Metropolis dynamics.

items.title: An SCL-Aware Design of PAC Codes
items.summary: We develop design methodologies for the rate profile of polarization-adjusted convolutional (PAC) codes tailored to successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding. The crux of our approach is two-fold: first is the creation of a modified density evolution Gaussian approximation (DEGA), called conditional DEGA (CDEGA), to analyze the decoding process in the presence of errors; second is the creation of a dangerous-path occupancy metric to find the conditional occupancy of bit-errors in a finite list. Our approach not only illuminates the role of rate-one precoding, but also provides insight into why certain information sets are particularly well suited to PAC codes. We demonstrate the usefulness of CDEGA and dangerous-path metrics with algorithms that create new information sets, as well as precoders that are extremely sparse yet competitive. In particular, we design codes of length $N \leq 512$ with various rates and list sizes, all of which offer at least half a dB gain over traditional PAC codes at an FER of $10^{-3}$ and improve upon state-of-the-art results.

items.title: Zero-freeness for Random Regular Graphs up to the Replica Symmetry Breaking Threshold
items.summary: We study antiferromagnetic spin systems on random regular graphs through the lens of the phase transitions characterized by the complex zeros of the partition function. Our motivating examples include the hardcore model and the antiferromagnetic Potts model (including proper $q$-colorings at $β=0$). For both models on random $d$-regular graphs, we establish, with high probability over the graph, zero-free regions throughout the interior of the replica-symmetric regime. Asymptotically, this regime extends up to tree occupation density $$α< α_{\mathrm{RSB}}(d) = (2\log d - 2\log\log d + 2 - 2\log 2 + o_d(1))/d$$ for the hardcore model and up to degree $$d < d_{\mathrm{RSB}}(q) = (2q-1)\log q - 2\log 2 + o_q(1)$$ for proper $q$-colorings. Leveraging the standard algorithmic implications of zero-freeness, we obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms that multiplicatively approximate the corresponding partition functions at fixed rational parameters throughout this regime, with high probability over the graph. Our algorithmic guarantees significantly improve upon prior work and extend beyond the parameter ranges reached by previously known search algorithms. To establish our results, we first develop reinforced small subgraph conditioning, which resolves short-cycle fluctuations in the complex plane by lifting classical small subgraph conditioning on random regular graphs to random holomorphic functions.
